stories.title: Real Capital Solutions Launches $350M Distressed Office Acquisition Fund
stories.excerpt: Real Capital Solutions (RCS), a real estate investment firm headquartered in Colorado, has launched a new $350 million fund that will target acquiring distressed Class A and Class B offices across the U.S., Commercial Observer can first report. The fund, RCS Contrarian Office Fund, plans to lever-up and ultimately acquire up to $850 million of office assets from the $350 million raised. The fund is already capitalized through a $50 million personal commitment by Marcel Arsenault, founder and CEO of Real Capital Solutions, and a second $47.5 million commitment from an unnamed entrepreneur. The fund will close in the first quarter of 2027. “While the office market continues to reset, we believe the long-term outlook for premier office assets is extremely strong,” Arsenault said in a statement. “Companies still need high-quality workplaces to attract tenants, foster innovation and drive growth, and those assets will continue to outperform over time.” This is not the first time RCS has jumped into pools of office distress. Since 2024, the firm has invested $644 million into acquiring 14 office properties in 10 U.S. markets — buildings that include Walnut Glen Tower and Tower at Park Lane in Dallas; Belleview Tower in Denver; Tysons Pointe in Northern Virginia; 101 Marietta Street in Atlanta; and the Equitable Building in Chicago, a 35-story Class A office tower the firm acquired earlier this year for $132.5 million, or a 77.8 percent discount to replacement cost. Adam Abeln, chief investment officer and managing director at RCS, credited the firm’s recent investment activity to a “contrarian approach” the firm has always taken, in remarks to CO. “Generally, we found you get rewarded when you have that contrarian outlook where pricing is disconnected from market fundamentals,” he said. “The whole office market today has been painted with the same brush, and the discounts go across the board, regardless if it’s trophy office or Class A, B or C buildings.” The
bullets: Real Capital Solutions launches $350M distressed office fund, targeting $850M in Class A/B acquisitions nationwide
Fund backed by $97.5M in founder and entrepreneur commitments; leverage strategy deployed across U.S.
Management signals belief in long-term office recovery, betting on flight-to-quality institutional-grade assets
stories.summary: Real Capital Solutions launched a $350 million distressed office fund with plans to acquire up to $850 million of Class A and Class B office assets across the U.S. through leverage. The fund is capitalized by $50 million from founder Marcel Arsenault and $47.5 million from an unnamed entrepreneur. Management believes premier office assets will outperform long-term despite current market headwinds.
stories.impact: Signals growing institutional capital targeting office distress and refinancing risk—critical context for multifamily developers in mixed-use submarkets where office conversion (or co-development) opportunity may emerge as office yields compress and adaptive reuse becomes economically viable. Watch for secondary markets where distressed office could unlock redevelopment capital.

stories.title: El-Ad National Buys Oceanfront Fort Lauderdale Hotel for $60M
stories.excerpt: Developer El-Ad National Properties has paid $60 million for an oceanfront hotel in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., property records show. The 99-room Sea Club Resort sits on a 1.2-acre site at 619 North Fort Lauderdale Beach Boulevard, between Belmar and Auramar streets. The 54,982-square-foot building dates back to 1954. An entity tied to Rachel Levy and Michael Man has owned the resort since 1995, when it paid just under $4 million for it. The entity provided $40 million in seller financing to El-Ad National Properties, a Boca Raton-based division of Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva’s El-Ad Group. The property will likely be redeveloped. Berkadia has been marketing the site as “one of the last remaining oceanfront development sites in the Fort Lauderdale area.” The land is zoned to house a 541-unit, 246,989-square-foot development up to 200 feet tall, according to Berkadia. An additional 40 feet could be granted if 60 percent of units serve as a hotel, though the Sea Club Resort’s lobby is protected under a preservation agreement with the Broward Trust for Historic Preservation. El-Ad is an active developer in South Florida. Last year, it nabbed an $85 million construction loan for a mixed-use, 2.8 million-square-foot development in Davie. That same year, it completed the luxury Alina Residences condo development in Boca Raton. A spokesperson for El-Ad did not respond to a request for comment. The sellers could not be reached for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: El-Ad National buys oceanfront Fort Lauderdale hotel for $60M; seller finances $40M of purchase
1.2-acre site zoned for 541-unit, 246,989-sf residential development up to 200 feet; 40-foot bonus if 60% units are hotel
Last remaining oceanfront development site in Fort Lauderdale; likely multifamily redevelopment ahead
stories.summary: Israeli developer El-Ad National Properties acquired the 99-room Sea Club Resort in Fort Lauderdale for $60 million, with the seller providing $40 million in financing. The 1.2-acre oceanfront parcel is zoned for a 541-unit residential development and is positioned as one of the last remaining oceanfront development opportunities in Fort Lauderdale, likely triggering redevelopment.
stories.impact: Scarce oceanfront land in Fort Lauderdale signals tight supply of premium development sites and validates aggressive pricing for last-remaining parcels—expect continued bid-up in South Florida coastal submarkets. El-Ad's financing flexibility and long-term hold mentality suggests development timing is multi-year; monitor absorption in adjacent rental communities to inform delivery phasing.

stories.title: Oxbow Adding 10 Retail Buildings to Pearl Project
stories.excerpt: Oxbow Development Group submitted plans to the city for 10 new retail buildings on either side of Avenue A. Along with completely new builds, the firm is seeking permission to demolish a vacant industrial building at 250 E. Grayson St.,. The new structures will add 85,000 square feet of space to the complex. The development is being led in a partnership between Oxbow and 3-O Real Estate Partners. The San Antonio Business Journal reports the joint venture is aiming for a mix of local, regional, national and global tenants that are a good fit for Pearl. Alamo Architects and Don B. McDonald Architects are designing the project. Oxbow plans to break ground in early 2027, expecting to finish construction in late 2028. Pearl Brewery Redevelopment features the transformational adaptive reuse of a 21-acre 1900s brewery into a mixed-use village. The post Oxbow Adding 10 Retail Buildings to Pearl Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Oxbow Development adds 10 retail buildings, 85,000 sf to Pearl mixed-use project in San Antonio
Groundbreak early 2027; construction completion late 2028; partnership with 3-O Real Estate Partners
Pearl Brewery adaptive reuse transformation continues expansion across 21-acre 1900s brewery site
stories.summary: Oxbow Development Group and 3-O Real Estate Partners submitted plans to add 10 new retail buildings totaling 85,000 square feet to the Pearl Brewery redevelopment in San Antonio. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027 with completion in late 2028. The project targets a mix of local, regional, national and global tenants across the 21-acre adaptive reuse site.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact; primarily retail expansion within existing mixed-use framework. However, Pearl's continued investment and long entitlement-to-delivery timeline (2027–2028) signals stable demand for mixed-use activation in San Antonio's central submarkets—potential supportive environment for adjacent residential infill, but no new demand signal for multifamily supply itself.

stories.title: Bezos’ Aerospace Company Could Land in Hutto
stories.excerpt: Construction of a manufacturing plant associated with Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin aerospace company may soon be a reality for Hutto, joining a host of other Central Texas spaceflight companies. The proposed Project Blue Hub plant will be about the size of 26 football fields – 1.3 million square feet at a cost of $650 million. It would be joining a host of other Central Texas spaceflight companies. Blue Origin is a competitor to Elon Musk’s SpaceX project, located in nearby Bastrop. The towns economic development agency has been working on financial incentives, should Blue Origin commit. If plans come to fruition, the deal could bring up to 2,000 jobs to the area. Blue Origin was established by Bezos in 2000 The post Bezos’ Aerospace Company Could Land in Hutto appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Blue Origin planning 1.3M-sf manufacturing plant in Hutto, Texas; $650M investment, ~2,000 jobs targeted
Project Blue Hub would establish major aerospace/defense hub in Central Texas near SpaceX (Bastrop)
Local incentives under negotiation; significant employment concentration risk and opportunity for job-driven migration
stories.summary: Blue Origin is considering a $650 million manufacturing facility in Hutto, Texas, spanning 1.3 million square feet and creating approximately 2,000 skilled jobs. The aerospace company's potential entry into Central Texas would add to the region's spaceflight ecosystem alongside SpaceX operations in nearby Bastrop. Hutto's economic development agency is negotiating financial incentives.
stories.impact: Major demand signal for Central Texas multifamily—2,000 skilled aerospace jobs in Hutto would drive inbound migration and household formation, lifting rents across Austin metro periphery and secondary markets (Hutto, Round Rock, Pflugerville). If Blue Origin commits, developers should prioritize entitled land within 20–30 minutes of manufacturing campus; construction employment could also lift costs regionally. Timeline remains uncertain pending deal close.

stories.title: Town Lane, Axis Partners Launch IOS Platform Venture
stories.excerpt: Town Lane, a New York-based real estate investment management firm, has acquired a 23-property industrial outdoor storage (IOS) portfolio and launched a platform venture with Axis Partners, an Atlanta-based industrial owner and operator. The transaction includes an investment by Town Lane in the Axis operating platform. Terms were not disclosed. The portfolio comprises mission-critical, infill IOS assets that support the day-to-day operations of local, regional, and national businesses, including contractors, equipment rental companies, distributors, infrastructure providers, and service businesses. It’s located in high-growth Sunbelt markets such as Atlanta, Houston, Dallas and Nashville. “The Axis team has built a differentiated sourcing and operating platform that consistently identifies mission-critical, off-market assets supporting the infrastructure behind local and regional economies,” said Garret Overlock, managing director at Town Lane. “This partnership provides a unique opportunity to combine institutional capital with an experienced operator, and we’re excited to build a market-leading platform together over the long term.” Pictured: An Axis Partners-owned IOS facility in Laredo, TX. The post Town Lane, Axis Partners Launch IOS Platform Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Town Lane, Axis Partners launch industrial outdoor storage (IOS) platform; 23-property acquisition in Sunbelt markets
Portfolio located in Atlanta, Houston, Dallas, Nashville; mission-critical infill assets supporting regional contractors/logistics
Institutional capital + experienced operator model; no transaction terms disclosed
stories.summary: Town Lane, a New York-based real estate investment firm, acquired a 23-property industrial outdoor storage portfolio and launched a platform venture with Axis Partners, an Atlanta-based operator. The portfolio comprises infill, mission-critical assets in high-growth Sunbelt markets including Atlanta, Houston, Dallas, and Nashville that support contractors, equipment rental companies, and service businesses.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily relevance. However, capital formation in niche industrial assets signals investor appetite for Sunbelt alternative real estate and reinforces that Atlanta, Houston, Dallas, Nashville remain top-tier capital destinations—competitive dynamic for multifamily land acquisition and development financing in these core markets. IOS assets often compete for infill land with multifamily; monitor competition for scarce urban parcels.

stories.title: James Marcellino Re-Joins Colliers’ New York City Office as Vice President
stories.excerpt: More than 13 years after departing Colliers as an associate director, James Marcellino has returned to the company’s New York office as a vice president. Starting today, Aug. 10, , Marcellino’s new role will focus on office leasing and tenant representation as Colliers continues expanding its New York presence, according to an announcement by the firm. John Gallagher, executive managing director for New York City at Colliers, called Marcellino’s return “another important step” in the firm’s growth. “His institutional ownership experience and entrepreneurial perspective will bring immediate value to our clients and our team, and we’re thrilled to welcome him back,” Gallagher said in a statement. The executive brings with him more than 17 years of experience advising institutional owners, landlords and occupiers on office leasing. In his most recent work as a real estate consultant, Marcellino advised the Bracha Group, Modernus Architectural Products, and Christie’s International Real Estate’s leading residential sales team, the Gottlieb Team. Marcellino previously served as vice president of leasing at L&L Holding Company from 2023 to 2024, according to the announcement. While there, he oversaw leasing strategy for its 6.3 million-square-foot portfolio and completed nearly 344,000 square feet of office and retail transactions. Marcellino first arrived at Colliers as an associate director in late 2011. He departed in 2013 for an associate role at CBRE, and eventually moved on to leasing leadership positions at CIM Group and the Moinian Group. “Colliers has built a tremendous platform in New York, and I’m excited to return at a time when clients are looking for thoughtful, experienced guidance on increasingly complex real estate decisions,” Marcellino said in a statement. “I’ve built my career on strong relationships and finding opportunities that create meaningful value for clients, and I’m excited to continue that work at Colliers.” Marcellino earned his un
bullets: James Marcellino rejoins Colliers NYC as Vice President; 17+ years office leasing and institutional asset experience
Colliers expanding New York office leasing presence; hire reflects firm's growth strategy in Manhattan market
Marcellino brings landlord and occupier expertise from L&L Holding, Bracha Group, and advisory roles
stories.summary: James Marcellino rejoined Colliers' New York office as Vice President, focusing on office leasing and tenant representation. With 17 years of experience advising institutional owners and occupiers, Marcellino previously held senior leasing roles at L&L Holding and recently worked as a real estate consultant for the Bracha Group and other institutional clients.
stories.impact: Minimal multifamily impact. Signals Colliers' confidence in NYC office market recovery and continued institutional leasing activity—relevant only if office-to-residential conversion opportunities accelerate in Manhattan submarkets. No direct demand, supply, capital, or cost signal for multifamily development.

stories.title: Westville To Open at 540 Third Avenue in Murray Hill
stories.excerpt: Westville is getting ready to open its 12th location in the U.S. and bring a selection of classic American foods to Manhattan’s Murray Hill neighborhood. The restaurant brand just signed a 4,148-square-foot lease at the base of 540 Third Avenue, also known as the Dian, a 22-story, 160-unit residential building at the corner of Third Avenue and East 36th Street, according to broker Meridian Capital Group. The lease comprises 2,739 square feet on the ground floor and 1,409 square feet on the lower level. The asking rent and the length of the lease were not disclosed, but the average asking rent for retail space in the nearby Herald Square area was $394 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. CBRE’s Robert Bonicoro and Betsy Da Silva represented Westville in the lease, while Meridian’s James Famularo and Jordan Langer represented ownership, which is a joint venture between Gilar Realty and Ranco Capital. CBRE did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. “Westville had its pick of locations in this market, and its decision to commit long-term at 540 Third Avenue underscores the continued demand for well-built, well-located retail on Third Avenue,” Langer said in a statement. Meridian did not disclose when Westville will open its new Murray Hill location. The franchise also has Manhattan restaurants in the West Village, Chelsea, the East Village, the Upper East Side and on Wall Street, as well as a spot in Long Island City, Queens. Westville opened its first location outside of New York City in Northern Virginia. “When Whole Foods and Westville commit to the same few blocks within months of each other, that is not a coincidence, it is a corridor being repositioned in real time,” Famularo said in a statement. “Ownership delivered a first-class space and held firm on value, and we brought in an operator that will draw customers from the day it opens.”
bullets: Westville restaurant signs 4,148-sf lease at 540 Third Avenue (Murray Hill); ground and lower-level space
Retail asking rent ~$394/sf in nearby Herald Square area (Q2 2026); mixed-use residential base at Dian building (160 units)
12th U.S. location for Westville; typical neighborhood-serving retail activation in Manhattan residential tower
stories.summary: Westville, a restaurant brand, signed a 4,148-square-foot lease at 540 Third Avenue in Murray Hill, comprising 2,739 square feet on the ground floor and 1,409 square feet on the lower level. The Dian, a 22-story, 160-unit residential building, serves as the host. Comparable Herald Square retail asking rents averaged $394 per square foot in Q2 2026.
stories.impact: Minimal multifamily impact. Demonstrates continued ground-floor retail tenancy confidence in Manhattan mixed-use residential buildings, supporting property value and stabilized rents. No demand, supply, capital, or development cost signal; standard neighborhood retail fill in established residential asset.

stories.title: Bristol Myers Squibb Chooses Houston for $2.3B Investment
stories.excerpt: Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) selected Houston as the site for a new, multi-modal manufacturing campus, representing an approximately $2.3 billion investment designed to accelerate the delivery of next-generation medicines to patients. The campus, at Generation Park in Houston, will create nearly 500 skilled jobs and is designed to grow in scale, capability and workforce for decades to come. The selection of Houston marks a significant milestone in BMS’ $40 billion commitment to invest in the United States over five years across research and development, technology and domestic manufacturing. The Houston campus will be modular and multi-modal. Its modular design allows BMS to add and reconfigure manufacturing capacity as needed, reflecting BMS’ current and future pipeline. Its multi-modal capabilities allow BMS to manufacture multiple types of medicines – such as small molecules, biologics, and antibody-drug conjugates – across a range of disease areas. Last year, Eli Lilly announced it would invest in a $6.5 billion active pharmaceutical ingredients plant, also in the Generation Park complex in Houston. bullets: Bristol Myers Squibb selects Houston Generation Park for $2.3B manufacturing campus; ~500 skilled jobs
Modular, multi-modal pharmaceutical manufacturing facility; part of BMS's $40B five-year U.S. investment commitment
Eli Lilly also investing $6.5B in Generation Park complex; Houston becomes major pharma/life sciences hub
stories.summary: Bristol Myers Squibb selected Generation Park in Houston for a $2.3 billion multi-modal pharmaceutical manufacturing campus that will create approximately 500 skilled jobs. The facility will support small molecules, biologics, and antibody-drug conjugates. This investment is part of BMS's $40 billion five-year U.S. commitment and follows Eli Lilly's announced $6.5 billion active pharmaceutical ingredients plant at the same complex.
stories.impact: Significant demand driver for Houston multifamily, particularly near Generation Park corridor. Combined BMS ($2.3B) + Eli Lilly ($6.5B) manufacturing commitments signal major employment concentration—estimate 500+ BMS jobs plus similar-scale Eli Lilly roles will draw skilled workforce inbound and boost household formation across Houston metro, especially Energy Corridor and southwest suburbs. Developers should acquire/entitle land within 15–20 minutes of Generation Park; expect sustained rent growth as job base stabilizes. Monitor construction cost inflation from dual major pharma campus build-out.

stories.title: Mamdani, MTA Look to Proptech Solutions to Cool Subways and Heat Buildings
stories.excerpt: The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) and Mayor Zohran Mamdani are considering high tech options to transfer heat out of subway stations and into the buildings above, in what would likely be a complicated and pricey infrastructure project. Still, city officials and the MTA believe it could be worth it to provide straphangers with a more comfortable wait on platforms, by using the heat generated below to cut energy to commercial and residential buildings above ground. “We are exploring a lot of possible options to make stations more comfortable,” MTA Chairman Janno Lieber said during a Monday press conference in the Chambers Street Station on the J and Z lines. “We’re looking into innovative energy networks called TENs and the geothermal concepts that will allow us to capture, store and then transfer the excessive heat in a subway station so that it can be used come the winter to heat the buildings upstairs.” While the technology has never been used in coordination with a transit system before, some buildings in New York City gather heat from below ground through geothermal technology, including St. Patrick’s Cathedral in Midtown and 555 Greenwich Street in Hudson Square. It is most widely used in Canada and Europe, according to Lieber, and proptech companies have been showcasing the use of geothermal piles as building infrastructure for several years now. It’s unclear what exactly the technology would look like on a grand scale or how many buildings it would serve, but city officials such as New York City Comptroller Mark Levine believe it could get complicated between city, state and private stakeholders. But it could be expanded to cultivate heat from grocery store refrigerators and small data centers scattered across the five boroughs. bullets: NYC MTA and Mayor Mamdani exploring thermal energy networks (TENs) to capture subway heat, transfer to buildings above
Geothermal/energy-capture infrastructure project; targets platform cooling and building heating via heat exchange
Technology untested in transit coordination; potentially expensive, complicated infrastructure retrofit with long development timeline
stories.summary: The NYC Metropolitan Transportation Authority and Mayor Zohran Mamdani are exploring thermal energy networks (TENs) and geothermal concepts to capture excess heat from subway stations and transfer it to commercial and residential buildings above ground. While the technology offers potential benefits for platform cooling and building-level efficiency, it has never been coordinated with a transit system and would likely require significant investment and complexity.
stories.impact: Long-term strategic signal for Manhattan multifamily developers: if TENs infrastructure materializes, it could reduce operating costs for residential buildings in dense transit-oriented markets and unlock development economics for previously marginal sites. However, timeline is uncertain and capital requirements unknown; monitor pilot projects. No near-term supply, demand, or financing impact; primarily a cost-efficiency opportunity for future multifamily operating margins in core Manhattan.

stories.title: Public/Private Partnership Could Net Opa-Locka 1,500 Rental Units, Retail, Hotel
stories.excerpt: DBJ&L and MRK Partners are working with the town of Opa-Locka to redevelop its historic downtown. The plan includes thousands of residential units and 275,000 square feet of retail. The S. Florida Business Journal reports the city’s community redevelopment agency voted in favor of a resolution that authorizes negotiations for a long-term ground lease involving the development group and six publicly owned properties. The developers seek to replace those buildings with 225 apartments, 50,000 square feet of flex space, a 35,000-square-foot grocery store, a 15,000-square-foot daycare facility and a 100-room hotel, as part of the first phase of development. Across all phases, the project would add about 1,500 residential units, including affordable housing, and 275,000 square feet of retail, plus the hotel, a structured parking garage and a new elementary school, all on more than 16 acres. Opa-Locka City Place would be one of the biggest projects in years in the city. The town had a population of about 16,000 people last year. The post Public/Private Partnership Could Net Opa-Locka 1,500 Rental Units, Retail, Hotel appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: DBJ&L and MRK Partners pursue 1,500-unit multifamily project in Opa-Locka (South Florida) via public-private partnership
Phase 1: 225 apartments, 50k-sf flex, 35k-sf grocery, 15k-sf daycare, 100-room hotel on 6 publicly owned properties
Full-build includes 1,500 units, 275k-sf retail, hotel, parking, elementary school across 16+ acres; ground lease structure
stories.summary: DBJ&L and MRK Partners are negotiating a long-term ground lease with Opa-Locka to redevelop six publicly owned properties in the city's historic downtown. Phase 1 will deliver 225 apartments, 50,000 square feet of flex space, a 35,000-square-foot grocery store, a 15,000-square-foot daycare, and a 100-room hotel. The full master plan encompasses 1,500 rental units (including affordable housing), 275,000 square feet of retail, parking, and an elementary school across 16+ acres.
stories.impact: Significant supply addition to South Florida multifamily market, particularly in Opa-Locka submarket. 1,500-unit pipeline signals aggressive infill/redevelopment activity in lower-density, underutilized corridors near Miami; municipal partnership de-risks entitlement and ground lease economics. Monitor absorption and rent trajectory as Phase 1 delivers (likely 2027–2029); competitive pressure on adjacent secondary markets. Affordable housing component and mixed-use retail/services indicate demand for workforce housing in Miami periphery. Early development signal for competing projects in Opa-Locka and similar Miami-Dade opportunity zones.
